variants.headline: Looking back: party divides in two
variants.sub: A split in {party} has produced the new party {splinter}.
variants.body:
We return to {first_reported}. Our report recorded this: The party {party} had split, with {splinter} the new breakaway party.

A party has split in two. A simple sentence for a very public break. There is no need to invent the private quarrel to make it interesting. Readers should ask what the division is for, and whether the people being represented will find something more useful than competing claims to loyalty.

The event remains part of the record. Whether subsequent developments met the standard it raised is a separate question, not something the old headline can answer by itself.

The responsibility of {target} should be considered without presuming the split's cause or its eventual consequences. This account records an organisational division and reserves judgment on particulars not supplied.

variants.headline: Looking back: a political organisation breaks apart
variants.sub: The new party {splinter} has broken away from {party}.
variants.body:

Time changes the distance from an event, not the need to judge it carefully. Any claim about improvement or deterioration needs more than a recollection of the original news.

variants.headline: Looking back: unity gives way to a party split
variants.sub: The party {party} has split, with {splinter} the new breakaway party.
variants.body:

What has changed since then should be examined against that original record. What has not changed is the need to distinguish an established event from the hopes or fears attached to it.
